lead: Superposition turns one hard circuit into several easy ones. In a linear circuit carrying more than one independent source, the voltage across or the current through any element equals the sum of the values that each source would produce on its own, with every other source set to zero. It exists so that a set of simultaneous equations can be replaced by a few small circuits solved with dividers. It is used in small-signal amplifier analysis, where a bias source and a signal add, and in fault studies, where several generators feed one point.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for independent and dependent sources, 1.3 for KCL and KVL, 1.4 for the divider rules, and 1.6 for one reliable solution method to check your answer against.

sections.h3: The idea and its two conditions

blocks.text: A circuit can carry more than one independent source: a 12 V supply, a 3 A current source, a signal generator. Superposition says you do not have to solve them together. Keep one source, set every other independent source to zero, and find the voltage or current you want. Repeat for each source. Add the results with their signs. The sum is the answer for the complete circuit.

Why it exists: a circuit with three sources usually needs one nodal or mesh solution with several unknowns, and every source sits inside every equation. Splitting it into three one-source circuits replaces that with three small reductions, each done quickly by series-parallel work. The theorem is the formal reason those small answers may be added.

items: Linear: every element has a straight-line relation between voltage and current, such as v = iR. A diode does not, so superposition fails there.
Bilateral: the element behaves the same with current in either direction. A resistor is bilateral; a transistor is not.

blocks.text: Switching a source off means setting its value to zero, not cutting the wire. A 0 V voltage source is a short circuit. A 0 A current source is an open circuit. These two source types are described in 1.2.
V = V′ + V″ + …   and   I = I′ + I″ + …
blocks.where: V and I are the voltage and current in the complete circuit; V′ and I′ are the parts produced by the first independent source acting alone, V″ and I″ by the second, and so on. The primes are labels, not derivatives.

sections.h3: The procedure, and where dependent sources go

blocks.text: Fix one reference direction first. Draw the arrow for the current you want on the full circuit and keep that same arrow in every partial circuit.

items: Pick the element whose voltage or current you want.
Keep one independent source. Replace every other independent voltage source by a short circuit and every other independent current source by an open circuit.
Solve the reduced circuit by series-parallel reduction, a divider, or one node equation.
Repeat for each independent source left in the original circuit.
Add the partial results with their signs, in the fixed reference direction.

blocks.text: Dependent sources stay in place in every partial circuit. A dependent source is not a driving source; its value is fixed by a voltage or current somewhere else, so it must be carried through every pass. Setting it to zero deletes part of the circuit and gives a wrong answer.

Watch the signs. If a partial current comes out opposite to your reference arrow, enter it as negative before adding. Two partial currents of 1.2 A in the same direction give 2.4 A; in opposite directions they cancel.

sections.h3: Voltage and current add, power does not

blocks.text: Superposition works because the circuit equations are linear. Power is not linear. If two partial currents of 1.2 A each flow in a 6 Ω resistor, the total current is 2.4 A and the power is 2.4² × 6 = 34.56 W. Adding the two partial powers gives 2 × (1.2² × 6) = 17.28 W, which is only half the true value.
So find the total current or voltage first, then square it. Never superpose power.
P = I²R = (I′ + I″)² R  ≠  I′²R + I″²R
blocks.where: I′ and I″ are the partial currents from each source acting alone, in amperes; R is the resistance in ohms; P is the power in watts. The missing power is the cross term 2I′I″R; in the 6 Ω example above it is 2 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 6 = 17.28 W.

blocks.text: One node equation is the check. In the figure the 12 V source feeds node A through 4 Ω, the 3 A source injects into A, and 6 Ω runs from A to ground. KCL at A gives (V − 12)/4 + V/6 = 3. Multiply by 12: 3V − 36 + 2V = 36, so 5V = 72 and V = 14.4 V. The superposition sum must land on the same number.

figure.caption: The complete two-source circuit is solved twice, once with the 3 A source opened and once with the 12 V source shorted. Each pass gives 1.2 A in the 6 Ω resistor, and the two add to 2.4 A.

spec.title: Superposition in three steps
spec.aria: The full two-source circuit splits into a sub-circuit with only the 12 V source and one with only the 3 A source, each giving 1.2 A, which are added at the end to 2.4 A.

examples.question: A 12 V voltage source feeds node A through a 4 Ω resistor. A 3 A current source injects current into node A. A 6 Ω resistor connects node A to ground. Using superposition, find the current in the 6 Ω resistor (from A to ground) and the voltage at node A.
steps: Reference: let I be the current in the 6 Ω resistor from A downwards, and V_A the node voltage. Keep both directions in every partial circuit.
Source 1 alone, 12 V on and 3 A off: the current source becomes an open circuit, so the circuit is 12 V, 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series. I′ = 12/(4 + 6) = 12/10 = 1.2 A. V_A′ = 1.2 × 6 = 7.2 V.

Source 2 alone, 3 A on and 12 V off: the voltage source becomes a short circuit, so the 4 Ω resistor now runs from node A to ground, in parallel with the 6 Ω. The 3 A divides between them: I″ = 3 × 4/(4 + 6) = 3 × 0.4 = 1.2 A. V_A″ = 1.2 × 6 = 7.2 V.
Add the partial results: I = 1.2 + 1.2 = 2.4 A downwards, V_A = 7.2 + 7.2 = 14.4 V.
Check with one node equation: (V_A − 12)/4 + V_A/6 = 3 gives 3V_A − 36 + 2V_A = 36, so 5V_A = 72, V_A = 14.4 V and I = 14.4/6 = 2.4 A. The two methods agree.
examples.answer: The current in the 6 Ω resistor is 2.4 A from A to ground, and the voltage at node A is 14.4 V.

traps: Superposing power. P = I²R is not linear; add the currents first, then square.
Switching off a dependent source. Dependent sources stay in every partial circuit because they are controlled by the circuit itself.
Deleting a source instead of zeroing it. A dead voltage source is a short circuit (0 V) and a dead current source is an open circuit (0 A); removing the branch changes the network.
Losing the sign. Fix one reference arrow at the start and enter a partial current as negative when it flows the other way.
Using the theorem on a circuit with a diode, a lamp or any non-linear element. The two conditions, linear and bilateral, must both hold.

quiz.q: State the superposition theorem and its two conditions.
quiz.a: In a linear, bilateral network with several independent sources, the voltage or current in any element equals the algebraic sum of the values produced by each source acting alone, all other independent sources set to zero. Conditions: the circuit is linear and the elements are bilateral.

quiz.q: Why is a dependent source not switched off during superposition, while an independent source is?
quiz.a: An independent source drives the circuit and can be set to zero to isolate one contribution. A dependent source only sets its value in a fixed ratio to some other voltage or current; it is part of the circuit's behaviour, not a driver. Zeroing it would remove an element and change every partial answer.

quiz.q: A 10 V source feeds node A through 5 Ω. A 2 A current source injects into node A, and a 5 Ω resistor connects A to ground. Use superposition to find the current in the grounded 5 Ω resistor.
quiz.a: 10 V alone, 2 A opened: I′ = 10/(5 + 5) = 1 A, V_A′ = 5 V. 2 A alone, 10 V shorted: the two 5 Ω resistors are in parallel, I″ = 2 × 5/(5 + 5) = 1 A, V_A″ = 5 V. Total I = 2 A and V_A = 10 V.

quiz.q: A student adds the two partial powers in the worked example and reports 17.28 W in the 6 Ω resistor. Identify the error and give the correct power.
quiz.a: Power is proportional to the square of current, so it is not linear and cannot be superposed. The total current is 2.4 A, so P = 2.4² × 6 = 34.56 W. The missing 17.28 W is the cross term 2I′I″R.

quiz.q: Why does superposition require bilateral elements?
quiz.a: Superposition assumes the response to a reversed source is the same magnitude with the opposite sign. In a non-bilateral element the resistance differs with the direction of current, so the partial answers cannot simply be added.

quiz.q: Two sources give partial currents of 3 A and 2 A in a branch, in opposite directions. What is the branch current?
quiz.a: Take the reference arrow along the 3 A partial current: I = 3 − 2 = 1 A in that direction.

quiz.q: Which single equation would you use to check a superposition answer in a two-node circuit?
quiz.a: A KCL node equation at the unknown node, written with the full set of sources in place. Solve it once; the node voltage must match the superposed value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators such as SPICE do not apply superposition directly; they assemble one matrix for the whole circuit and solve it at once. The linearity argument returns in small-signal analysis of amplifiers (see Unit 4, Semiconductor Devices and Analog Circuits), where the DC bias and the tiny AC signal are handled separately and then added. Power-system fault studies use the same idea, summing each generator's contribution to a fault current. Searches worth trying: linear network, small-signal superposition, fault current contribution.
